answer.rationale: p99 write-path latency at 5× target, confined to the primary region, while settlement writes are at daily peak. The release two hours ago is a plausible trigger (pattern matches memory_b1), but a rollback takes time to propagate and does not immediately relieve the already-stressed primary; during settlement peak, every minute of elevated write latency risks queuing, timeouts, or dropped customer writes. memory_b2 records that regional failover during a prior latency degradation restored latency fast, shifted traffic cleanly, and recovered error rates within minutes—directly analogous to a single-region write-path degradation. Choosing failover over rollback because: (1) the degradation is region-scoped, so moving traffic to the secondary region removes load from the degrading primary immediately; (2) it preserves all in-flight and new customer writes without requiring a build re-deploy cycle; (3) capacity headroom is already proven (memory_b3 pattern); (4) once the secondary absorbs traffic, the primary can be investigated and the suspect release rolled back in the next intervention window without customer pressure. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) protect against partner outages, not internal write-path latency. Read-replica routing (memory_b5) helps dashboard read load, not the write path under settlement pressure. Staged gating (memory_b6) is a preventive control, not a live mitigation.
